prose.summary: An exhibit designer plans how a space tells a story: where a visitor stands, what they see first, what the label says versus what the object says on its own. It sits next to interior design and set design but the brief is different, because the thing being designed has to survive a school group leaning on it and still make sense to someone who reads only the first line of every label.
prose.day_to_day: The week starts with a schedule, usually, because 25% of postings name it directly: which vendor delivers casework on which day, when the graphics proof comes back, when the gallery goes dark for install. Most days split between drawing (plans, elevations, sometimes a quick SketchUp model to check a sightline) and sitting in a room with curators, fabricators, or a collections manager arguing gently about whether a case needs UV glass. There is real solo time blocking out a floor plan or revising a label draft for the fourth time. The moment people wait for is walkthrough: the first time you stand in the finished gallery, before the public gets in, and see whether the path moves people the way the drawing said it would. Paperwork exists (condition reports, vendor quotes) but it is not the center of the job. The center is standing in the space and adjusting it before anyone else sees it.
prose.work_environment: This is not a remote job (0% of postings offer it), and the reason is physical: you need to be in the gallery, at the table with the model, or on site when the crate opens. Hours track the install calendar more than a clock, with weeks before an opening running long and weeks after running quiet. A bad week is a delayed shipment two days before a donor preview, or a fabricator who read the drawing wrong and cut the panel short. The setting is part office (drafting, email, scheduling) and part workshop or gallery floor (measuring, checking finishes, standing under bad lighting to see if a color reads the way it did on screen).
prose.getting_in: Most postings ask for an associate degree or equivalent as the entry credential, and 75% of postings state an experience requirement, with the median sitting at just one year. That one year is the real stall point: it usually gets built through an internship or assistant role at a museum, aquarium, or design firm rather than through more schooling. The degree itself does not take long to clear once you are in a design or museum studies program, and portfolio work can often start before graduation. Employers accept a strong portfolio of built or rendered exhibit work in place of a design pedigree, so a science center internship counts for more than a second degree.
prose.ladder: Early on you own a single case or a single wall: what goes in it, how it is lit, what the label says. The step up is owning a gallery, meaning you are the one deciding the visitor's path through six or eight cases and defending that sequence to a curator who wants it different. Past that, the fork is between staying the person who draws and details the space (and gets better at it, project after project) or moving into managing the exhibit program across multiple shows at once, which is more budget and vendor conversations than drafting. That fork tends to show up once someone has run a full install cycle or two on their own.
prose.suits: People who come alive here are the ones who like standing in a room and noticing that the label is six inches too high for a wheelchair user, or that the light hits the glass wrong at 2pm. It rewards someone who can hold both a floor plan and a fabrication drawing in their head at the same time, and who does not mind that a project takes eight months from concept sketch to opening night. The people who leave usually wanted faster feedback loops, closer to graphic design or web work where you see results in days, not seasons. If you want your name on something a stranger walks through, unannounced, on a Tuesday afternoon, this holds up over years in a way that a lot of design work does not.
prose.misconceptions: People assume this is decorating, arranging things so they look good. It is closer to writing a script for a room: sequence, pacing, what the visitor learns first versus last, and whether they can find the exit. The other misconception is that it is mostly digital, rendering pretty 3D walkthroughs. Most of the job happens at the intersection of a drawing and a real, physical constraint, like a doorway that is two inches narrower than the plan assumed.
prose.who_qualifies: No measured route into this role stands out in current postings, but the people who tend to land it come from museum studies, interior design, or theatrical set design backgrounds. Set design carries over the instinct for sightlines and sequencing under a hard deadline, but not the conservation and accessibility knowledge a museum expects. Interior design carries over drafting and materials fluency, but exhibits ask for more storytelling discipline, because the client is a visitor who did not ask to be there.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows what it feels like to open a case you built two years ago and find a kid with their face pressed against the glass. It also cannot show how much of the job is negotiation, getting a curator, a fabricator, and a budget to agree on the same wall.

steps.do: Get a design or museum studies degree
steps.how: An associate degree covers the entry bar most postings state; a bachelor's in exhibit design, museum studies, or interior design goes further. This typically runs two to four years and should include at least one studio course where you design a real installable space, not just a rendering.

steps.do: Build a portfolio of built work
steps.how: Assemble three to five projects that show a floor plan, a section drawing, and a photo of the built result, even at student scale. Museums hiring for entry roles want to see that a drawing of yours became a real object someone walked past.

steps.do: Take an internship at a museum or firm
steps.how: Look for an unpaid or stipended internship at a science center, aquarium, or design firm that fabricates for museums; these usually run three to six months and are the fastest way to the one year of experience most postings expect.

steps.do: Learn the fabrication side, not just design
steps.how: Spend time on a shop floor or with a vendor watching how casework gets built: materials, joinery, glazing, lighting mounts. This closes the gap between a drawing that looks right and one that survives install.

steps.do: Apply once you can show one full install
steps.how: Target roles once your portfolio includes at least one project taken from concept through opening day, even a small one. This is the credential that substitutes for years of tenure at many hiring institutions.

prose.tools: Visual design software (SketchUp, AutoCAD, Adobe Creative Suite) is the real gatekeeper; postings expect you to bring a finished set of drawings, not learn the software on the job. Scheduling tools matter almost as much, since coordinating fabricators and install dates is named in a quarter of postings directly. 3D modeling and rendering are becoming more standard for client pitches before a project is approved, but the hand-drafting instinct (proportion, human scale) still shows up in how work gets judged.

industries.name: History and science museums
industries.note: Longest project timelines, heaviest emphasis on accuracy and accessibility, slowest pace between shows.

industries.name: Aquariums and zoos
industries.note: Design has to survive humidity, animal proximity, and constant foot traffic; durability decisions dominate.

industries.name: Corporate and trade show exhibits
industries.note: Fast turnaround, weeks not months, and the work gets torn down and rebuilt repeatedly rather than living permanently.

industries.name: Design and fabrication firms
industries.note: You work across multiple client institutions at once, so variety is higher but you rarely see the long-term life of a piece you designed.

specializations.name: Accessible and universal design
specializations.why: Institutions increasingly require ADA-compliant sightlines, tactile elements, and multi-sensory exhibits, and designers fluent in this get pulled into every project a museum runs, not just one.

specializations.name: Interactive and digital exhibit integration
specializations.why: Touchscreens, projection mapping, and sensor-triggered elements are showing up more in postings, and designers who can spec the hardware as well as the case around it are scarce.

specializations.name: Traveling exhibit design
specializations.why: Designing for disassembly and shipping is a distinct skill from designing for a fixed gallery, and firms that produce touring shows pay for designers who get the crating and reinstall logistics right the first time.

pros: You get to stand in a finished room you designed and watch a stranger read it correctly without help.
The work mixes drafting, materials knowledge, and storytelling in a way that few design jobs combine in one role.
A finished exhibit tends to last years, so your work has a longer physical life than most design output.
Every project is a different subject (dinosaurs, submarines, civil rights history), so the research itself stays interesting.
cons: Projects run long, often eight months or more, so the feedback loop between decision and result is slow.
Budgets get cut mid-project more often than in other design fields, and the redesign lands on you.
The job requires being on-site for install, so travel or long on-location weeks come with the territory.
There is essentially no remote option, since the work depends on physical space and physical materials.

faq.q: how long does it take to become an exhibit designer
faq.a: Most people clear it in two to four years: a degree program plus roughly one year of hands-on experience, which is the median most postings state directly. The one year of experience is usually the slower part, since it depends on landing an internship or assistant role, not just finishing coursework.

faq.q: do you need a degree to be an exhibit designer
faq.a: Most postings ask for at least an associate degree, but a portfolio of built or rendered exhibit work matters more than which degree you hold. Museum studies, interior design, and theatrical design backgrounds all show up in this field regularly.

faq.q: exhibit designer vs interior designer, what's the difference
faq.a: Interior design is about how a space functions and feels for people who live or work in it; exhibit design is about how a space teaches or narrates something to someone passing through once. The drafting skills overlap heavily, but exhibit work adds storytelling sequence, label writing, and accessibility standards that interior design does not center on.

Rarely. None of the current postings offer remote work, because the job requires being physically present for site measurements, material selection, and install oversight that can't be done from a screen.

faq.q: is exhibit design a good career right now
faq.a: It suits people who want to see their design work exist physically and last for years, not just ship and move on. Openings are limited and concentrated (current postings are US-based and few in number), so it rewards patience in the job search as much as skill in the studio.
